A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpikePingpong system. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison, with components identifiable across renaming and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original robot experiments measuring contact prediction errors, target-return accuracy, sequential performance, and inference latency in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: V2 reports original robot evaluations, including updated precision results, relocated-launcher tests, human adaptation and transfer, ablations, and appendix failure analysis.

M1.justification: The filter history and calibration model's temporal input increase from three to ten frames (v1 Section 4.1 and Appendix C.2; v2 Appendices C.2 and E). This is a limited input-context change. The physics predictor, SONIC/System 2 correction network, IMPACT architecture, and MSE objectives are otherwise retained; the Fast-Slow terminology mainly regroups existing components.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation at two unseen off-center launcher positions and adaptation using Person A's demonstrations followed by transfer to unseen Person B. These extend the represented trajectory distributions and human-interaction scenarios. V1 already described human gameplay qualitatively, but lacked these distinct adaptation and transfer evaluations.

E2.justification: The single-target comparison removes LFP and GoalsEye and adds state-input variants of ACT and Diffusion Policy. V2 also adds physics-only and RNN contact-error comparisons, RNN ablations, a human sequential baseline, and a literature-reported HYSR comparison at 10 cm. The earlier without-SONIC ablation is retained as System 1 + IMPACT, rather than simply removed.

E3.justification: Calibration samples increase from 0.5k to 1k, temporal history changes from three to ten frames, and sequential evaluation changes from 20 shots to 100 with 25 targets per region. V2 adds vision/state input comparisons, accelerated 10-step DDIM evaluation, a 100-demonstration human adaptation protocol, and a 10 cm accuracy threshold. The newly disclosed 80/10/10 split does not establish a changed split.

E4.justification: V2 substantially extends the original component ablations with RNN alternatives, relocated-launcher robustness tests, and seen/unseen-human transfer analysis (Tables 1 and 5–7). Appendix G adds a failure taxonomy and measured failure proportions. Figure 5 adds an RGB-versus-spike capture comparison; the existing detection and EMA trajectory illustrations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions already report standard deviations for model accuracies. V2 additionally supplies standard deviations for the previously point-only human single-target comparison (v1 Table 2 versus v2 Table 3). Neither version specifies experimental repeat counts or seeds, or reports confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Reported single-target averages change from 91%/71% to 92%/70%, and overall contact MAE/RMSE from 2.47/3.13 to 12.34/13.85. The without-correction single-target result changes from 85% to 23%. Sequential performance changes from 95% for 20 shots to 78% for 100 shots; Diffusion Policy latency changes from 2437.22 to 25.18 ms under revised evaluation. New generalization, 10 cm, and failure-distribution results are added. These are updated or newly reported results, not established same-setting gains or losses.

T1.justification: The ballistic equations, MSE objectives, EMA equations, pixel-to-distance calculations, and interception pseudocode retain their mathematical substance. The new cognitive Fast-Slow analogy supplies conceptual motivation, not new formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: V2 makes cognitively inspired Fast-Slow perception the central contribution and adds claims about emulating human perception and applicability to industrial, medical, and aerospace systems. V1 emphasized SONIC/IMPACT precision and quantified superiority over prior systems. V2 removes the explicit 38/37-point superiority claims and revises the headline accuracy and sequential-performance claims.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new OOD and human-transfer results as evidence against memorization and individual-player overfitting. Appendix G newly attributes near-misses to unmodeled spin and contact timing sensitivity, and discusses implications of different failure categories. The existing spin and human-adaptability limitations are retained and expanded in Appendix H.

D1.justification: V2 clarifies that deployment does not require spike-camera feedback, specifies the 80/10/10 split and one-shot inference scheduling, and states that code is supplied in supplementary material with public release planned; availability cannot be verified from the PDFs. Most hardware, annotation, and training details are retained or relocated into Appendix E. The earlier spike-frame saving interval is omitted.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work around Kahneman's dual-system theory and Moravec's paradox, with new citations connecting it to industrial, medical, and aerospace applications. It also adds recent robotic table-tennis work, including D'Ambrosio et al. (2025) and Su et al. (2025), while removing several trajectory-planning and LFP references. This exceeds a bibliographic update.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, and method exposition are extensively rewritten around Fast-Slow terminology. Method subsections are regrouped, experiments are consolidated into main results and ablations, and the appendices are reorganized and expanded. Ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: Framework diagrams are regrouped and relabeled, Figure 1 replaces its spatial success display with a bar chart, and contact examples are revised. The landing-distribution Figure 5 is removed and a different camera-comparison Figure 5 added. Tables are substantially restructured and expanded with generalization, ablation, precision, and failure displays, alongside an ICLR layout conversion.

improvement.justification: V2 improves empirical scrutiny through optimized baseline evaluations, explicit distribution-shift and human-transfer tests, and quantified failure analysis, making applicability boundaries clearer than in v1. The gains are limited by removing LFP/GoalsEye comparisons and introducing unresolved numerical inconsistencies: Table 7's sequential overall rates of 15% and 52% fall below every corresponding regional rate. These problems weaken the new ablation evidence, although the broader generalization evaluation remains informative.
